review_notes: No exact regulatory claim beyond artifact workflow.
post_body:
Quick check:

Can every active grant answer these four questions today?

- Award amount
- Period of performance
- Next report due
- Evidence folder location

If one answer lives in the CRM, one in accounting, one in a spreadsheet, and one in someone's inbox, Monday starts with reconciliation instead of management.

export_pattern: donor CRM to general ledger reconciliation
review_notes: Uses source guide reconciliation workflow; no aggregate claim.
post_body:
The donor CRM and the grant ledger can describe the same funder in different languages.

Development sees Foundation X as a relationship, proposal, award letter, and pledge.

Finance sees a receipt, restriction, fund code, release schedule, and reporting obligation.

Neither view is wrong.

The risk starts when they do not meet.

A monthly reconciliation should match:

- funder name
- award amount
- cash received to date
- restriction classification
- grant status
- source document

The source document matters most. If the grant agreement says restricted, the CRM tag should not say unrestricted general support.

review_notes: Board reporting fields sourced from guides.
post_body:
Board week gets easier when the grant page answers the board's real question:

Are we on track, and where do we need to pay attention?

That means active award amount, percent spent, percent of time elapsed, restricted balance, next report due, and any open compliance issue.

Not every transaction.

review_notes: CTA count within daily cap; resource title from lead-magnet seed bank.
post_body:
Audit prep should not start with a shared drive search.

The useful binder starts with the PBC list, then maps every request to a named file, owner, and source record.

The GrantPipe Audit Prep Week-by-Week Checklist breaks the work into a calmer sequence:

- 90 days before fieldwork
- 60 days before fieldwork
- 30 days before fieldwork
- fieldwork week

Free download, no email required: grantpipe.com/resources/audit-prep-week-by-week-checklist.

review_notes: Checklist mirrors audit evidence binder sections.
post_body:
Six things that belong in the grant audit binder before fieldwork starts:

1. Notice of award and amendments
2. Grant ledger report
3. SF-425 or funder financial reports already submitted
4. Budget vs. actual summary
5. Time and effort records for grant-funded staff
6. Procurement records for major purchases

That list is not glamorous. It is the difference between "here is the support" and "we think that file is in a folder somewhere."

The binder is not a performance.

It is a map from every claim in the grant file to the document that supports it.

export_pattern: SF-425 cash drawn vs general ledger quick check
review_notes: SF-425 line 10e claim sourced from local guide.
post_body:
SF-425 line 10e deserves more respect than it gets.

That line is the federal share of expenditures. On a final SF-425, it is cumulative from the start of the award through the end of the period of performance.

Before submission, compare it to the grant-specific general ledger.

If the form and the ledger do not match, do not explain it later.

Find the variance before the report goes out.

That is the cleaner audit trail.

review_notes: ASC 958 release framing sourced from guide.
post_body:
Release from restriction is not new revenue.

Under FASB ASC 958, a release moves donor-restricted net assets into without-donor-restrictions when the purpose or time restriction has been met.

That distinction matters in board reporting.

A $100,000 grant can be real, restricted, and unavailable for general operations at the same time.

The schedule should show what was received, what remains restricted, what was released, and what condition triggered the release.

review_notes: Product claim stays at workflow and module boundary level.
post_body:
"One record" is not the same as "one login."

A team can buy five tools with single sign-on and still have five competing versions of the grant story.

The harder question is data shape:

Does the award connect to the fund?

Does the fund connect to spend-down?

Does spend-down connect to the report?

Does the report connect to evidence?

That is the operating problem GrantPipe is built around.

review_notes: 2 CFR 200 cost principle language sourced from local guides.
post_body:
Allowable is not enough.

For a federal grant cost to survive 2 CFR 200 review, it also has to be allocable, reasonable, consistently treated, and adequately documented.

The allocable part is where messy work hides.

If rent, payroll, software, or supplies benefit multiple programs, the split needs a documented basis.

Convenience is not a cost allocation method.

Time worked, square footage, headcount, or another reasonable basis is much easier to defend.

review_notes: No product mention; operational board utility post.
post_body:
Executive Directors do not need a 30-row transaction dump in the board packet.

They need the grant portfolio view:

- active awards
- restricted balances
- budget spent vs. time elapsed
- next reporting dates
- open compliance concerns
- renewals or gaps in the next 12 months

The board can govern from that.

Staff can keep the transaction detail where it belongs.

review_notes: CTA count within daily cap; resource slug sourced from guide.
post_body:
Donor-to-grant reconciliation is boring until the numbers disagree in public.

The template should answer:

- What did Development enter?
- What did Finance record?
- What does the award document say?
- Is the amount pledged, awarded, received, or released?
- Who changed the record after review?

GrantPipe has a Donor-to-Grant Reconciliation Template for teams cleaning up CRM, fund, and grant records before board or audit season.

Free download, no email required: grantpipe.com/resources/donor-to-grant-reconciliation-template.

export_pattern: donor CRM to general ledger reconciliation
review_notes: Uses source guide example, rewritten as structural timing issue.
post_body:
The phrase "the CRM says $75,000, but the ledger says $50,000" is not a finance argument.

It is a timing question.

Award amount, pledged amount, and received-to-date amount are different fields.

When they share one field, the reconciliation meeting becomes detective work.

review_notes: Product data model claim grounded in product context.
post_body:
We model grants and funds as separate records in GrantPipe.

That choice is slower to build, but it matches the work.

One grant can fund several restricted funds.

One fund can support work tied to several awards.

A donor restriction can outlive a reporting deadline.

An award can close while the financial statement still needs the right restriction history.

For grant-funded nonprofits, flattening that into one "grant" object makes the early screen simpler and the later audit trail worse.

review_notes: Grants.gov claim follows approved boundary.
post_body:
Grants.gov search is only the front door.

For federal awards, the harder operating work starts after the opportunity becomes an award:

- UEI and SAM.gov details
- period of performance
- ALN or FAIN
- reporting cadence
- indirect cost basis
- pass-through or direct award status
- closeout deadline

GrantPipe includes Grants.gov federal opportunity search.

The post-award record is where the compliance work has to hold together.

review_notes: Hypothetical workflow prompt, no unsupported claim.
post_body:
Before you close Monday:

Pick one active award and open the evidence folder.

Can someone outside the grant team find the award letter, current budget, last financial report, last program report, and support for the largest expense?

If not, the issue is not the folder.

The issue is that the evidence trail depends on memory.

review_notes: 2 CFR 200.306 double-counting claim sourced from guide.
post_body:
Match tracking fails quietly.

The grant can look healthy on spend-down while the required recipient share is behind.

For every match requirement, keep a separate ledger:

- cash match
- in-kind match
- valuation basis
- source document
- grant period date
- already claimed elsewhere: yes or no

That last line matters. Under 2 CFR 200.306, the same match cannot satisfy two federal awards.

review_notes: ASC 958 donor-restricted vs board-designated distinction sourced from guide.
post_body:
Donor-restricted is not the same as board-designated.

Under ASC 958, donor restrictions come from outside the organization. The board can designate funds internally, but it can also change that designation later.

That difference should show up in the schedule.

If the board packet merges both into "restricted," the cash picture gets muddy fast.

review_notes: Volunteer log and rate-basis requirements sourced from guide.
post_body:
If a match file has volunteer time in it, check the dates first.

Contemporaneous logs are the point.

A year-end summary that says "volunteers contributed 400 hours" is not the same as signed records showing who worked, when, for how long, and on what activity.

The cleaner standard:

Log the time when the work happens.

Document the rate basis when the value is assigned.

Tie both to one award.

review_notes: Restricted fund schedule fields grounded in ASC 958 guide.
post_body:
The restricted fund schedule should be readable by someone who was not in the close meeting.

For each fund:

- opening restricted balance
- new restricted gifts or grants
- releases from restriction
- ending restricted balance
- restriction purpose
- source document

If the schedule needs oral history to explain it, it is not ready for board or audit use.

review_notes: Strong checklist slot; no CTA.
post_body:
Five match documents I would want before closeout:

1. The award term that creates the match requirement
2. Cash match ledger by date and source
3. In-kind logs signed by the contributor
4. Valuation support for donated services, space, or goods
5. A note showing the match was not claimed on another federal award

The uncomfortable part is that none of this is difficult.

It just has to exist before closeout pressure starts.

review_notes: FFATA threshold and timing sourced from local guide.
post_body:
FFATA reporting is easy to miss because it sits beside, not inside, the usual monitoring routine.

If you are the prime recipient and obligate a federal subaward of $25,000 or more, the report is due through SAM.gov by the end of the month after obligation.

The record needs the FAIN, subrecipient UEI, obligation amount, place of performance, and other required fields.

That is separate from 2 CFR 200.332 monitoring.

Same subaward. Different obligation.

review_notes: No product mention; board dashboard guidance sourced.
post_body:
A board grant dashboard should not look like a funder report.

The board is not approving every invoice.

It needs to see exposure, pacing, restriction, and risk:

- how much is active
- how much is restricted
- what is behind plan
- what report is near due
- what needs leadership attention

That is enough to govern without asking staff to perform a spreadsheet tour.

review_notes: Product claim limited to connected records from product context.
post_body:
Your CRM may know the funder relationship.

Your accounting system may know the cash.

Your shared drive may know the award letter.

Your spreadsheet may know the report due date.

The reconciliation burden is created by the gaps between those records.

GrantPipe's bet is simple: donor records, grants, restricted funds, evidence, and reporting should be connected from the start.

review_notes: CTA 1 of 3 for day; match checklist claim sourced.
post_body:
Grant match has two traps:

The first is cash flow. Can the organization actually supply the required share during the grant period?

The second is proof. Can it show the cash, in-kind value, date, rate basis, and award assignment later?

The Grant Compliance Checklist includes a match documentation section for federal awards.

That is a product decision and a trust decision.

The buyer still has hard work to do:

review_notes: Classification risk sourced from reconciliation guide.
post_body:
The donor record can say "general support" while the award letter says "restricted to youth STEM programming."

The award letter wins.

That is why Development and Finance need a shared review point before a restricted gift becomes board packet data.

The classification is not clerical.

It changes what the organization can spend, release, and report.

review_notes: CTA 2 of 3 for day; resource title from seed bank.
post_body:
If your audit binder is just a folder tree, it is missing the hard part.

The hard part is knowing which document answers which auditor request.

GrantPipe's Auditor Evidence Checklist is built around that mapping:

- request
- owner
- source record
- file name
- status
- reviewer note

Free download, no email required: grantpipe.com/resources/auditor-evidence-checklist.

review_notes: Identifier guidance is conservative and non-statistical.
post_body:
ALN replaced CFDA, but old language sticks around.

That sounds small until a federal award appears one way in the grant file, another way in the SEFA workpaper, and a third way in the board packet.

Pick the identifier format the award uses now.

Keep the legacy reference if it helps.

Do not let identifiers become another reconciliation project.

review_notes: Hypothetical board-prep question; no unsupported claim.
post_body:
Before the board meeting, ask one plain question:

Which grant would create the most trouble if a report, renewal, or spend-down issue landed this week?

That is the grant that belongs in the narrative section.

The rest can stay in the table unless it needs a decision.

review_notes: P7 without CTA to keep CTA cap at 2; scene explicitly hypothetical.
post_body:
Picture this:

An in-kind match file has signed volunteer logs, but no rate basis.

The hours happened.

The work mattered.

The value is still hard to defend.

For donated services, space, supplies, or equipment, the file needs the valuation support at the time the contribution is recorded.

review_notes: CTA 1 of 3 for day; restricted fund review grounded in ASC 958 source.
post_body:
Restricted fund cleanup is easier when the month-end checklist is specific.

The useful version asks:

- Which restricted balances changed?
- Which releases were recorded?
- Which award documents support the restriction?
- Which balances need board explanation?

GrantPipe's Restricted Fund Month-End Close Checklist gives the review a simple shape.

Free download, no email required: grantpipe.com/resources/restricted-fund-month-end-close-checklist.

export_pattern: SF-425 cash drawn vs general ledger quick check
review_notes: SF-425 Box 10e and ledger reconciliation sourced.
post_body:
An SF-425 should come from the ledger.

Not from last quarter's form.

Not from a guessed spend-down percentage.

Not from the number that feels close enough.

Run the grant-specific report, check cumulative federal expenditures, compare cash drawn, then submit.

If Box 10e and the grant ledger disagree, the report is not ready.

review_notes: Restricted fund schedule structure grounded in ASC 958 guide.
post_body:
The cleanest restricted fund schedule has a boring shape:

Opening balance.

New restricted revenue.

Releases.

Ending balance.

Source document.

Restriction type.

That boring shape is a gift to the Executive Director, the board treasurer, and the auditor reading your internal shorthand for the first time.

review_notes: Grants.gov boundary follows product context.
post_body:
Federal opportunity search is not the same as federal grant management.

Search helps you find the NOFO.

Management starts when the award creates:

- a period of performance
- approved budget
- reporting cadence
- payment method
- indirect cost rule
- closeout deadline

GrantPipe includes Grants.gov federal opportunity search.

It also treats post-award records as first-class work.

review_notes: Strong checklist slot; product workflow claim sourced.
post_body:
Four records I want connected before a grant becomes active:

1. The award record
2. The restricted fund record
3. The reporting calendar
4. The evidence folder

That is the minimum operating map.

The award tells you what was promised.

The fund tells you what can be spent.

The calendar tells you when the funder expects an answer.

The evidence folder proves the answer.

review_notes: Advance drawdown and reimbursement claims sourced from guide.
post_body:
Cost reimbursement creates a cash timing problem.

The organization spends first, documents the expense, submits the request, then waits for payment.

Advance drawdowns are different. Under 2 CFR 200.305, federal cash advances are tied to immediate need, and excess cash creates interest obligations.

That means the grant file should track more than spend-down.

It should also track request dates, payment dates, and aging reimbursement status.

review_notes: Status flag examples derived from board dashboard guide.
post_body:
Board reporting gets sharper when every grant has a status flag.

Not a mood. A defined flag.

On track: spend and time are aligned.

Needs attention: pacing, documentation, or renewal risk needs leadership review.

Compliance issue: a missed report, finding, late submission, or unresolved funder request exists.

The definitions matter more than the colors.

review_notes: Many-to-many grants and funds claim grounded in product context.
post_body:
We built GrantPipe around a many-to-many relationship between grants and funds.

That is not a database flourish.

It is how the work behaves.

One program can be funded by a federal award, a foundation grant, and donor-restricted gifts.

One grant can support several funds or cost centers.

If the model cannot express that, the spreadsheet comes back.

review_notes: CTA 1 of 3 for day; resource title from guide library.
post_body:
Grant closeout is easier when the file already knows what closeout requires.

Final financial report.

Final program report.

Final draw or reimbursement request.

Equipment disposition notes if applicable.

Unspent balance decision.

Record retention date.

The Grant Closeout Checklist puts those items in one review path.

Free download, no email required: grantpipe.com/resources/grant-closeout-checklist.

review_notes: No product mention; renewal dependency framed as workflow logic.
post_body:
The development calendar and the compliance calendar should talk to each other.

A renewal deadline is not just a fundraising task.

It may depend on whether the last report was accepted, whether spending is on pace, whether match is current, and whether evidence is clean.

That is why grant operations cannot live only in the donor CRM.

review_notes: CTA 2 of 3 for day; resource title from seed bank.
post_body:
The Award Setup Worksheet is for the moment right after "we got the grant."

That is when the record should capture:

- funder
- award amount
- restriction
- period of performance
- budget categories
- reporting cadence
- payment method

Free download, no email required: grantpipe.com/resources/award-setup-worksheet.

export_pattern: access controls and nonprofit data security
review_notes: Reviewer access boundary follows role guidance and product context.
post_body:
Access controls are part of grant operations.

An auditor or funder reviewer may need grant, fund, document, compliance, accounting, and report access.

They do not need donor records, billing, team settings, or admin controls.

That is why GrantPipe's reviewer access is intentionally scoped.

Read-only should mean read-only in the right part of the system.

review_notes: Founder voice constraint and no fake proof policy followed.
post_body:
I do not want GrantPipe copy to pretend the company has ten years of nonprofit operator history.

It does not.

The honest claim is narrower:

We are building from the workflow shape, the reporting requirements, the accounting standards, and the product decisions we can defend.

That means public pricing, no setup fee, no borrowed credibility, and a trial that has to stand on its own.

review_notes: SEFA fields are conservative and artifact based.
post_body:
The SEFA is not just an audit schedule.

It is a test of whether federal award data has been maintained all year:

- federal agency
- pass-through entity, if any
- ALN
- FAIN or award number
- federal expenditures
- subrecipient amounts

If that data has to be rebuilt at audit time, the audit is now doing the job the operating system should have done earlier.

review_notes: Short artifact check; no unsupported claim.
post_body:
Wednesday night check:

Open one active grant and ask whether a new staff member could understand it in 10 minutes.

They should see the award, fund, budget, deadline calendar, last report, and evidence status without asking who "owns the spreadsheet."

That is the bar.
